title: In Search of Freedom: Stories of Afghanistan Exhibition
description: In Search of Freedom: Stories from Afghanistan  OPEN SEPTEMBER 4, 2026 - DECEMBER 4, 2026, MONDAY - FRIDAY 12-4 PM  OPEN 5-8 PM ON FIRST FRIDAYS OF THE MONTHIn Search of Freedom: Stories from Afghanistancelebrates the beauty, resilience, and rich cultural heritage of Afghanistan through an exhibition of oil paintings by Afghan artist Qahar Behzad, alongside the collaborative mural,August 15: A Mural for Afghanistan.Organized in partnership with Indiana University's Center for Refugee Studies and Exodus Refugee Immigration, the exhibition explores the humanity of the refugee experience through the lens of Afghanistan, inviting visitors to look beyond conflict and discover the stories and experiences of displaced people.The exhibition brings together Qahar's vibrant paintings - which honor Afghanistan's history, traditions, and everyday beauty - withAugust 15: A Mural for Afghanistan,a collaborative project led by Tiffany Black Behzad in collaboration with 59 Afghan evacuees at Camp Atterbury following the fall of Afghanistan to the Taliban on August 15, 2021. Developed through art therapy workshops with Afghan artists Zainab Ahmadi and Fawzia Abdaly, the mural preserves the participants' voices, memories, hopes, and resilience. The mural stands as a record of collective experience and a tribute to those who continue to seek safety, dignity, and freedom against all odds.Together, the artworks present a deeply human portrait of displacement, resilience, and belonging, inviting visitors to reflect on the the universal connections that unite us across borders, traditions, and generations, and the enduring human desire for freedom.

title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.

title: Byrnes Institute Colloquium Book Talk: "The Bolsheviks Survive: Petrograd 1919" with Janet Rabinowitch and Tatiana Saburova
description: Petrograd, the imperial capital and the urban stage upon which virtually the entire Russian Revolution was enacted, in 1919 struggled through a year of civil war, hunger, social upheaval, and political and economic challenges. Based on exhaustive research in previously closed Russian archives, Alexander Rabinowitch authoritatively presents an in depth look at how Petrograd's local Soviet government and Bolshevik Party organizations struggled to implement the Bolshevik Party program, fight domestic and foreign counterrevolutionaries, quiet labor unrest, and provide food, fuel, and education to the local population. The methods and strategies used by the government and party organizations to organize public life and fight enemies, domestic and foreign, not only preserved the infant Soviet regime but proved to be the first manifestation of what would become the one-party authoritarian Soviet political system.

title: Rethinking Refugee Integration: Evidence from Newly Resettled Afghans in the United States
description: U.S. refugee policy continues to emphasize rapid employment and economic self-sufficiency as primary indicators of successful integration. Drawing on a program of research with newly resettled Afghan households in Missouri and Oregon, this presentation examines refugee integration through a multidimensional lens that extends beyond employment and income.  Using survey data from Afghan households in St. Louis, Missouri (N = 184) and Portland, Oregon (N = 150), alongside a national sample of refugee households from the Annual Survey of Refugees (N = 1,386), we examine multidimensional deprivation and its determinants among refugees resettled in the United States. Findings reveal widespread multidimensional deprivation, affecting 62% of households in St. Louis, 74% in Portland, and 70% of the national refugee sample. Household size and English language proficiency emerged as consistent predictors of deprivation across settings. At the same time, local contexts mattered: lower housing costs and greater economic security in St. Louis were associated with lower rates of multidimensional deprivation compared with Portland.  To better understand how refugees experience integration beyond material conditions, we draw on a follow-up mixed-methods study of 203 Afghan households and five focus group discussions. Quantitative findings indicate that stronger social connectedness within Afghan communities was associated with higher quality of life, whereas integration with Americans was not. Qualitative findings revealed strong intra-ethnic social ties alongside limited bridging connections to the broader host society. Participants described declining quality of life during the first five years of resettlement despite a strong sense of community belonging.  Together, these findings challenge employment-centered approaches to refugee integration and highlight the importance of multidimensional frameworks that account for material well-being, social connectedness, and quality of life. location: The Comedy Attic, 123 S Walnut Street, Bloomington, IN
description: Introducing Denny Love, a Los Angeles–based actor and comedian whose career seamlessly bridges prestige television, live comedy, and viral digital culture. A celebrated alumnus of DePaul University’s renowned Theatre School, Denny first broke through with a standout performance in Hulu’s Looking for Alaska, a critically acclaimed series boasting a 92% Rotten Tomatoes rating. He went on to appear in two seasons of Taylor Sheridan’s hit Paramount+ drama Mayor of Kingstown, further solidifying his dramatic range. Beyond the screen, Denny is a commanding live performer who has shared stages with comedy heavyweights like Chris D’Elia and delivered memorable sets opening for Theo Von. As a key cast member of @KevinLangue’s viral YouTube and TikTok content, he has helped build a digital powerhouse of over 4.47 million subscribers and more than 2 billion views worldwide. Denny Love’s live stand up presence is rapidly becoming one of the most exciting forces in comedy. He’s been taking the comedy scene by storm by performing at the most coveted venues in and around the LA area, across the country and internationally. Most notably; The Laugh Factory, The Comedy Store, Improv, Haha Comedy Club, Comedy Chateau, Jam in the Van, Don’t Tell Comedy, Can’t Even, and many more. He recently headlined at the Tokyo Comedy Bar in Tokyo, Japan and ROR Comedy Club in Osaka, Japan. Denny was seen on stages all across America and Canada while on tour with Chris D’elia and most recently in Las Vegas with Theo Von. In 2026, he takes the stage at Netflix Is a Joke, solidifying his place among the most sought-after rising voices in entertainment. This summer, he joins the Kevin Langue Show as a key performer on an ambitious 18- city national theatre tour, bringing his sharp timing and undeniable charisma to audiences across the country. Building on that momentum, Denny will launch his first headlining tour in Fall 2026, marking a major milestone as he steps fully into his own spotlight.

title: Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma | Additional Films and Guests
description: Visionary director Jane Schoenbrun (I Saw the TV Glow) presents a new kind of horror remake in Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma. Bursting with imagination and surreal wit, their latest genre-bending wonder affirms there's no such thing as a guilty pleasure. After years of slapdash sequels and waning fandom, the Camp Miasma slasher franchise is due for resurrection. And one young director (Hannah Einbinder) is more than up to the task. But when she visits the original's star, a now-reclusive actress (Gillian Anderson), the two women fall into a blood-soaked world of desire, fear, delirium—under threat from the spear-wielding Little Death. Winner of the Queer Palm, this transformative Cannes favorite leads its protagonists to true fulfillment, encouraging us to ask how we can reach our own. [112 min; horror; English]

title: Daniel Luis Martinez: The Blueprint | Exhibition
location: The Contemporary Art Museum of Indianapolis
description: Opening reception: Friday, October 2, 2026, 6–10pm  Exhibition on view: October 2–December 18, 2026  For this exhibition, the blueprint is used as both a representational and conceptual departure point. Daniel Luis Martinez uses cyanotype printmaking and mixed-media drawing techniques as a generative process to imagine a speculative home on the CAMi campus. The hybrid drawings and prints featured in the exhibition explore the tactile middle-ground of the blueprint as a creative endeavor.  The series employs orthographic conventions typical of architectural drawing sets, though not as precise instructions for building. Rather, a layered and loose approach expresses ideas of home as an architectonic language.  Daniel Luis Martinez is a registered architect, educator, and co-founder of the multi-disciplinary design studio LAA Office, which explores the intersection of landscape, art, and architecture. His research and creative work investigate the potential of public art to generate alternative forms of placemaking. Martinez is Associate Professor and Director of the IU Eskenazi School's J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program (https://architecture.indiana.edu/index.html) in Columbus, Indiana.  Learn more about the exhibition at the CAMI website (https://camindy.org/exhibitions-all/theblueprint).
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Frances Lightbound: The Land Dissolves in Water | Exhibition
description: Lecture: October 27, 6:30–8pmExhibition: October 27–December 6, 2026, Mon.–Thur. 10am–4pm when IU classes are in session  Lightbound studies the production of space in urban environments, weaving narratives across photography, print, spatial interventions, and sculpture, with a focus on materials and sites in transition.  Architecture becomes an entry-point to questions of land use, ownership and access, bodily experience and perception, and timeframes ranging from the human to the geological. Lightbound invites viewers to consider and participate in the continual (re)construction of meaning in urban environments.  Frances Lightbound holds a B.A. from Glasgow School of Art, Scotland, and an M.F.A. from the School of the Art Institute of Chicago. Recent solo exhibitions include Louise Hopkins Center for the Arts (Lubbock, TX), RULE Gallery (Marfa, TX), and the John David Mooney Foundation (Chicago, IL); her work has been exhibited internationally at venues in London, Glasgow and Berlin. Lightbound is a Lecturer at School of the Art Institute of Chicago in the departments of Print media and Photography.The J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program Lecture and Exhibition Series brings prominent working artists and architects to Columbus. Lectures take place in the auditorium and exhibitions in the gallery, both located within The Republic Building, 333 Second Street in Columbus. The gallery is open Monday through Friday from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. All events are free and open to the public.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

description: Introducing Denny Love, a Los Angeles–based actor and comedian whose career seamlessly bridges prestige television, live comedy, and viral digital culture. A celebrated alumnus of DePaul University’s renowned Theatre School, Denny first broke through with a standout performance in Hulu’s Looking for Alaska, a critically acclaimed series boasting a 92% Rotten Tomatoes rating. He went on to appear in two seasons of Taylor Sheridan’s hit Paramount+ drama Mayor of Kingstown, further solidifying his dramatic range. Beyond the screen, Denny is a commanding live performer who has shared stages with comedy heavyweights like Chris D’Elia and delivered memorable sets opening for Theo Von. As a key cast member of @KevinLangue’s viral YouTube and TikTok content, he has helped build a digital powerhouse of over 4.47 million subscribers and more than 2 billion views worldwide. Denny Love’s live stand up presence is rapidly becoming one of the most exciting forces in comedy. He’s been taking the comedy scene by storm by performing at the most coveted venues in and around the LA area, across the country and internationally. Most notably; The Laugh Factory, The Comedy Store, Improv, Haha Comedy Club, Comedy Chateau, Jam in the Van, Don’t Tell Comedy, Can’t Even, and many more. He recently headlined at the Tokyo Comedy Bar in Tokyo, Japan and ROR Comedy Club in Osaka, Japan. Denny was seen on stages all across America and Canada while on tour with Chris D’elia and most recently in Las Vegas with Theo Von. In 2026, he takes the stage at Netflix Is a Joke, solidifying his place among the most sought-after rising voices in entertainment. This summer, he joins the Kevin Langue Show as a key performer on an ambitious 18- city national theatre tour, bringing his sharp timing and undeniable charisma to audiences across the country. Building on that momentum, Denny will launch his first headlining tour in Fall 2026, marking a major milestone as he steps fully into his own spotlight.

title: Daniel Luis Martinez: The Blueprint | Exhibition
location: The Contemporary Art Museum of Indianapolis
description: Opening reception: Friday, October 2, 2026, 6–10pm  Exhibition on view: October 2–December 18, 2026  For this exhibition, the blueprint is used as both a representational and conceptual departure point. Daniel Luis Martinez uses cyanotype printmaking and mixed-media drawing techniques as a generative process to imagine a speculative home on the CAMi campus. The hybrid drawings and prints featured in the exhibition explore the tactile middle-ground of the blueprint as a creative endeavor.  The series employs orthographic conventions typical of architectural drawing sets, though not as precise instructions for building. Rather, a layered and loose approach expresses ideas of home as an architectonic language.  Daniel Luis Martinez is a registered architect, educator, and co-founder of the multi-disciplinary design studio LAA Office, which explores the intersection of landscape, art, and architecture. His research and creative work investigate the potential of public art to generate alternative forms of placemaking. Martinez is Associate Professor and Director of the IU Eskenazi School's J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program (https://architecture.indiana.edu/index.html) in Columbus, Indiana.  Learn more about the exhibition at the CAMI website (https://camindy.org/exhibitions-all/theblueprint).
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Frances Lightbound: The Land Dissolves in Water | Exhibition
description: Lecture: October 27, 6:30–8pmExhibition: October 27–December 6, 2026, Mon.–Thur. 10am–4pm when IU classes are in session  Lightbound studies the production of space in urban environments, weaving narratives across photography, print, spatial interventions, and sculpture, with a focus on materials and sites in transition.  Architecture becomes an entry-point to questions of land use, ownership and access, bodily experience and perception, and timeframes ranging from the human to the geological. Lightbound invites viewers to consider and participate in the continual (re)construction of meaning in urban environments.  Frances Lightbound holds a B.A. from Glasgow School of Art, Scotland, and an M.F.A. from the School of the Art Institute of Chicago. Recent solo exhibitions include Louise Hopkins Center for the Arts (Lubbock, TX), RULE Gallery (Marfa, TX), and the John David Mooney Foundation (Chicago, IL); her work has been exhibited internationally at venues in London, Glasgow and Berlin. Lightbound is a Lecturer at School of the Art Institute of Chicago in the departments of Print media and Photography.The J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program Lecture and Exhibition Series brings prominent working artists and architects to Columbus. Lectures take place in the auditorium and exhibitions in the gallery, both located within The Republic Building, 333 Second Street in Columbus. The gallery is open Monday through Friday from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. All events are free and open to the public.

It's On Us is required for all first-year and transfer undergraduate students. You must attend one session to fulfill the requirement.

The Writers Guild is thrilled to host award-winning graphic novelist Nate Powell for our December 6 First Sunday Prose Reading Series. PLEASE NOTE: NEW LOCATION: REDBUD BOOKS at 408 W. Kirkwood Avenue https://www.google.com/maps/search/408+W.+Kirkwood+Avenue?entry=gmail&source=g . Nate will read a portion of his newest work, Diana, a prequel to his last graphic novel, Fall Through. Images from Diana will be up on screen. Audience members may purchase his books at this event.

Nate Powell is a National Book Award-winning cartoonist who began self-publishing comics as an Arkansas teenager in 1992.

His work includes the new graphic novel Diana, a prequel to his last book, Fall Through, and a comics adaptation of James Loewen’s Lies My Teacher Told Me, as well as Save It For Later, civil rights icon John Lewis’ March trilogy and its follow-up Run, viral comics essay About Face, and graphic novels Come Again, Two Dead, Any Empire, and Swallow Me Whole. He has published nonfiction comics and written for The Washington Post, The Nib, Popula, Booklist, CNN, and The Weather Channel.

Powell’s work has also received a Robert F. Kennedy Book Award, multiple Eisner and Ignatz Awards, ALA and YALSA distinctions, the Comic-Con International Inkpot Award, and the CXC Transformative Work Award. He has discussed his work at the United Nations, as well as on MSNBC’s The Rachel Maddow Show, CNN, NPR, PBS, and Free Speech TV.

From 1992 to 2010, he performed and toured in multiple underground punk bands including Soophie Nun Squad and Universe, and managed DIY label Harlan Records.

title: Daniel Luis Martinez: The Blueprint | Exhibition
location: The Contemporary Art Museum of Indianapolis
description: Opening reception: Friday, October 2, 2026, 6–10pm  Exhibition on view: October 2–December 18, 2026  For this exhibition, the blueprint is used as both a representational and conceptual departure point. Daniel Luis Martinez uses cyanotype printmaking and mixed-media drawing techniques as a generative process to imagine a speculative home on the CAMi campus. The hybrid drawings and prints featured in the exhibition explore the tactile middle-ground of the blueprint as a creative endeavor.  The series employs orthographic conventions typical of architectural drawing sets, though not as precise instructions for building. Rather, a layered and loose approach expresses ideas of home as an architectonic language.  Daniel Luis Martinez is a registered architect, educator, and co-founder of the multi-disciplinary design studio LAA Office, which explores the intersection of landscape, art, and architecture. His research and creative work investigate the potential of public art to generate alternative forms of placemaking. Martinez is Associate Professor and Director of the IU Eskenazi School's J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program (https://architecture.indiana.edu/index.html) in Columbus, Indiana.  Learn more about the exhibition at the CAMI website (https://camindy.org/exhibitions-all/theblueprint).
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: Daniel Luis Martinez: The Blueprint | Exhibition
location: The Contemporary Art Museum of Indianapolis
description: Opening reception: Friday, October 2, 2026, 6–10pm  Exhibition on view: October 2–December 18, 2026  For this exhibition, the blueprint is used as both a representational and conceptual departure point. Daniel Luis Martinez uses cyanotype printmaking and mixed-media drawing techniques as a generative process to imagine a speculative home on the CAMi campus. The hybrid drawings and prints featured in the exhibition explore the tactile middle-ground of the blueprint as a creative endeavor.  The series employs orthographic conventions typical of architectural drawing sets, though not as precise instructions for building. Rather, a layered and loose approach expresses ideas of home as an architectonic language.  Daniel Luis Martinez is a registered architect, educator, and co-founder of the multi-disciplinary design studio LAA Office, which explores the intersection of landscape, art, and architecture. His research and creative work investigate the potential of public art to generate alternative forms of placemaking. Martinez is Associate Professor and Director of the IU Eskenazi School's J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program (https://architecture.indiana.edu/index.html) in Columbus, Indiana.  Learn more about the exhibition at the CAMI website (https://camindy.org/exhibitions-all/theblueprint).
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: Daniel Luis Martinez: The Blueprint | Exhibition
location: The Contemporary Art Museum of Indianapolis
description: Opening reception: Friday, October 2, 2026, 6–10pm  Exhibition on view: October 2–December 18, 2026  For this exhibition, the blueprint is used as both a representational and conceptual departure point. Daniel Luis Martinez uses cyanotype printmaking and mixed-media drawing techniques as a generative process to imagine a speculative home on the CAMi campus. The hybrid drawings and prints featured in the exhibition explore the tactile middle-ground of the blueprint as a creative endeavor.  The series employs orthographic conventions typical of architectural drawing sets, though not as precise instructions for building. Rather, a layered and loose approach expresses ideas of home as an architectonic language.  Daniel Luis Martinez is a registered architect, educator, and co-founder of the multi-disciplinary design studio LAA Office, which explores the intersection of landscape, art, and architecture. His research and creative work investigate the potential of public art to generate alternative forms of placemaking. Martinez is Associate Professor and Director of the IU Eskenazi School's J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program (https://architecture.indiana.edu/index.html) in Columbus, Indiana.  Learn more about the exhibition at the CAMI website (https://camindy.org/exhibitions-all/theblueprint).
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: ACES Horizon Talk: "Spring Fever in the Gobi: Labor, Economy, and Care in Cashmere Harvest Interactions" by Dr. Kathryn Graber
description: The Association of Central Eurasian Students (ACES) warmly invites you to our upcoming Horizon Talk, featuring Dr. Kathryn Graber. Join us for an engaging discussion titled "Spring Fever in the Gobi: Labor, Economy, and Care in Cashmere Harvest Interactions."     In Mongolia's rural herding economy, it is difficult to overstate the importance of the spring cashmere harvest. For most herding families, cashmere is the main source of cash income for the year. So before their goats begin to naturally shed, herders quickly comb them, capturing the valuable undercoat from millions of animals nation-wide over a few feverish weeks.  Combing sessions are about more than extraction, however. This talk examines human-goat and human-human interactions during combing sessions in the Gobi to show what else is achieved in these moments: sharing labor, aligning perception, working out property relations, and caring for both the animals and each other.     Sponsored by: Central Eurasian Studies (CEUS) and the Inner Asian and Uralic National Resource Center (IAUNRC).     Please note that this event will be in person only. There will not be a Zoom or hybrid option. Lunch will be provided.

title: Open Studio
location: SIDNEY AND LOIS ESKENAZI MUSEUM OF ART
description: Our Open Studio program invites participants to create in the museum's art studio, where art becomes a tool for reflection, expression, and connection. Guided by a trained art therapist, the open studio welcomes visitors to engage with materials at their own pace while drawing inspiration from the surrounding exhibitions. No art experience is needed; just bring your curiosity and a desire to create, and we'll handle the rest!  Participants are welcome to utilize supplies located in the studio, as well as bring their own supplies/projects to work on.  This group meets on the 2nd and 4th Wednesday of every month, excluding holidays and museum closures. It is open to everyone: students, staff, and the public included! The group will meet in the Roehm Family Art-making Studio, located inside the Simpson Center for Education on the 2nd floor of the Eskenazi Museum of Art.

Bach: Prelude and Fugue in B Major, BWV 892 Unsuk Chin: Six Etudes (2003)Beethoven: Sonata in A-Flat Major, Op. 110 (1821)Montgeroult: Selections from "114 études de difficultés progressives"Beethoven: Sonata in C Minor, Op. 111 (1822)About the ArtistJeremy Denk is one of America's foremost pianists, hailed by the New York Times (NYT) as "a pianist you want to hear no matter what he performs" and celebrated for performances of vast imagination, beauty, profundity, and wit. An NYT bestselling author, Denk is the recipient of both the MacArthur "Genius" Fellowship and the Avery Fisher Prize and is a member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences. This season, Denk marks the bicentennial of Beethoven's death with a series of recitals across the United States, including appearances at Boston's Vivo Performing Arts, Philadelphia Chamber Music Society, and New York's 92nd Street Y. He also performs Beethoven at Carnegie Hall with the New York String Orchestra and Michael Stern, Brahms with the Vancouver Symphony, and Bartók with the St. Louis Symphony and Dinis Sousa. Denk continues his relationship with Scotland's Lammermuir Festival, where he performs six Mozart Piano Concertos, Schubert, and Janáček. He also continues his collaboration with the Takács Quartet, with performances including at Carnegie Hall, Cal Performances, and Santa Monica's BroadStage. Denk is celebrated for his original and insightful writings on music, which New Yorker critic Alex Ross praised for its "arresting sensitivity and wit." His NYT bestselling memoir, Every Good Boy Does Fine, was published to universal acclaim by Random House in 2022, with features on CBS Sunday Morning, NPR's Fresh Air, NYT, and TheGuardian. He also wrote the libretto for a comic opera presented by Carnegie Hall, Cal Performances, and the Aspen Festival, and his writing has appeared in TheNew Yorker, New Republic, Guardian, Süddeutsche Zeitung, and on the front page of the NYT Book Review. Denk is known for his interpretations of the music of Charles Ives, and in celebration of the 150th anniversary of his birth, Nonesuch Records released a collection of his Ives recordings in 2024. His recording of the Beethoven sonata was selected by BBC Radio 3's Building a Library as the best available version recorded on modern piano.

title: Daniel Luis Martinez: The Blueprint | Exhibition
location: The Contemporary Art Museum of Indianapolis
description: Opening reception: Friday, October 2, 2026, 6–10pm  Exhibition on view: October 2–December 18, 2026  For this exhibition, the blueprint is used as both a representational and conceptual departure point. Daniel Luis Martinez uses cyanotype printmaking and mixed-media drawing techniques as a generative process to imagine a speculative home on the CAMi campus. The hybrid drawings and prints featured in the exhibition explore the tactile middle-ground of the blueprint as a creative endeavor.  The series employs orthographic conventions typical of architectural drawing sets, though not as precise instructions for building. Rather, a layered and loose approach expresses ideas of home as an architectonic language.  Daniel Luis Martinez is a registered architect, educator, and co-founder of the multi-disciplinary design studio LAA Office, which explores the intersection of landscape, art, and architecture. His research and creative work investigate the potential of public art to generate alternative forms of placemaking. Martinez is Associate Professor and Director of the IU Eskenazi School's J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program (https://architecture.indiana.edu/index.html) in Columbus, Indiana.  Learn more about the exhibition at the CAMI website (https://camindy.org/exhibitions-all/theblueprint).
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: HIV/STI Testing
description: Free HIV Testing & Safer Sex Supplies at the LGBTQ+ Culture Center  Taking care of your sexual health is an important part of your overall well-being, and we're committed to making resources accessible, welcoming, and judgment-free.Positive Link (https://iuhealth.org/find-medical-services/positive-link-hiv-services) provides free and confidential HIV testing in Room 204 of the LGBTQ+ Culture Center every Thursday from 10:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. during the academic year. During the summer, testing is available on the first and third Thursdays of each month.  In addition, during the academic year, the Monroe County Health Department offers free chlamydia and gonorrhea testing on the third Thursday of every month, also from 10:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. in Room 101.  The LGBTQ+ Culture Center also offers a variety of free safer sex supplies, including condoms, internal condoms, dental dams, lubricants, and educational materials on proper use. These resources are available to all students, free of charge. You can find them in the kitchenette area near the back entrance of the Center and are welcome to take what you need.  STI Testing & Safer Sex Resources Beyond Campus  Prioritizing your sexual health should be simple and accessible. In addition to services available at the LGBTQ+ Culture Center, students can receive testing on campus through the IU Student Health Center (https://healthcenter.indiana.edu/medical/sti-testing/index.html) or visit several local organizations (https://healthcenter.indiana.edu/health-answers/sexual-health/sti-testing-resources.html) that offer free or low-cost testing and prevention services.  Many of these providers offer confidential care, safer sex supplies, and supportive information about prevention, treatment, and sexual wellness. If you're unsure where to start, we're happy to help connect you with resources that fit your needs.All Indiana University events, groups, activities, educational, cultural, and historical observances welcome all members of the Indiana University community.

title: Scholarly Write-In
description:
Write and work in solidarity with other IU scholars. We offer a silent work environment with coffee and natural light. The write-in is open to all graduate students (at any stage of their degree program).

We will check in at the beginning of our meeting, set some goals together, then work independently for a few hours. Fifteen minutes prior to the close of the meeting, we will reconvene to update each other on our progress and set broad goals for the coming week.

This is a casual meeting – feel free to come for as much or as little time as you like, and only during the weeks that work for you. You are welcome and encouraged to work on anything that you need time and space for: participants regularly work on dissertations, course papers, syllabi and lesson plans, articles and pieces for publication, and grading. Our goal is to create a space where we can work together in solidarity on whatever projects we need to each week.

Meets weekly throughout the semester, Thursdays from 1-4pm. No meeting during Thanksgiving break.

Co-sponsored by Writing Tutorial Services and the IU Libraries.

description:
Free Show! Music from 7-9
Nashville, TN duo Haunted Like Human delves into inspired songwriting, sparse arrangements, and frisson-inducing harmonies that mark their music. With a background in poetry and prose, Dale Chapman’s granular focus on language is simpatico with Cody Clark’s background in classical guitar, where each note carries its own weight. Limned with nostalgia, soaked in Southern gothic lore, the duo meticulously assembles songs to preserve the spirit of the stories they tell.
Praise for their new album American Mythology:
-“Proof that contemporary Americana still knows how to articulate, with rare sensitivity, the almost imperceptible scars that time leaves us.” – Music For All
-“Haunted Like Human build their characters and settings so clearly that the mood-inducing magic of the music makes you feel that you’re witnessing storytelling as focused on American soil as upon our long, shared human history.” – Americana Highways
-“Through its piercing limericks about human existence in all its shades, from downtrodden tumbleweeds to love-strewn epics, the record arrives at a time when everything feels so hopeless. It’s within their art that you can discover slivers of hope that can reignite the thirst for living.” – Rainbow Rodeo

title: Daniel Luis Martinez: The Blueprint | Exhibition
location: The Contemporary Art Museum of Indianapolis
description: Opening reception: Friday, October 2, 2026, 6–10pm  Exhibition on view: October 2–December 18, 2026  For this exhibition, the blueprint is used as both a representational and conceptual departure point. Daniel Luis Martinez uses cyanotype printmaking and mixed-media drawing techniques as a generative process to imagine a speculative home on the CAMi campus. The hybrid drawings and prints featured in the exhibition explore the tactile middle-ground of the blueprint as a creative endeavor.  The series employs orthographic conventions typical of architectural drawing sets, though not as precise instructions for building. Rather, a layered and loose approach expresses ideas of home as an architectonic language.  Daniel Luis Martinez is a registered architect, educator, and co-founder of the multi-disciplinary design studio LAA Office, which explores the intersection of landscape, art, and architecture. His research and creative work investigate the potential of public art to generate alternative forms of placemaking. Martinez is Associate Professor and Director of the IU Eskenazi School's J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program (https://architecture.indiana.edu/index.html) in Columbus, Indiana.  Learn more about the exhibition at the CAMI website (https://camindy.org/exhibitions-all/theblueprint).
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: Crystal Gale
description: Crystal Gayle is a beloved country music icon whose reign in the music business includes 22 No. 1 country hits, four Top 20 pop hits, six albums certified Gold by the RIAA and three certified Platinum, including We Must Believe in Magic which was the first album by a female artist in country music history to reach platinum sales. Her list of platinum and gold is matched by her awards and accolades. CMA’s “Female Vocalist of the Year” for two consecutive years, Crystal is also a Grammy® Award winner for “Best Female Vocal Performance” thanks to her timeless, international smash hit “Don’t It Make My Brown Eyes Blue” – a song that she today admits she has never grown tired of singing. Crystal has three Academy of Country Music Awards statuettes for “Top Female Vocalist” and won four American Music Awards. Not surprisingly, she was named the Most Performed Country Female Artist on radio for the decade of 1975-1985. Perhaps nothing sums up Crystal’s career achievements better than being awarded with a star on the fabled Hollywood Walk of Fame in October 2009. Famous for her nearly floor-length hair, Crystal was voted one of the 50 most beautiful people in the world by People Magazine and in 2016 the Academy of Country Music honored her with the Cliffie Stone Pioneer Award. Gayle was inducted into the Grand Ole Opry in January 2017 by her sister and Opry legend Loretta Lynn. For more information, visit crystalgayle.com ( http://crystalgayle.com/ ).

title: Grant Writing 101 and Public Funding for the Arts
location: SIDNEY AND LOIS ESKENAZI MUSEUM OF ART
description: Have a big artistic vision, passion project, or community arts idea—and zero clue how to pay for it? Or maybe you need introductory skills in understanding the application process for your future career?  Forget dry lectures and confusing jargon. This interactive session breaks down the real-world basics of getting your creative work funded. We'll cover:Decoding Public Funding: How city, state, and federal arts funders work—and how to find opportunities built for emerging artists and organizers.  Making Data Your Superpower: How to gather and use compelling data to back up your creative vision and make your grant applications stand out from the pile.  Zero experience is required!Whether you've never looked at a grant application in your life or just want to level up your resume, this workshop builds the foundational skills you need to start applying with confidence.  This workshop kicks off a three-part series designed to take you through the entire funding journey, continuing in Spring 2027. You can attend just one workshop or join us for all three!Workshop 1 (December 11):Grant Writing 101 & Public Funding for the Arts  Public funding essentials (city, state, federal) and using data to strengthen your application.  Workshop 2 (Spring 2027):Foundation Funding for the Arts — Exploring local and regional foundation opportunities, building genuine funder relationships, and crafting a standout story.  Workshop 3 (Spring 2027):Communicating Impact in the Arts and Culture Sector — Mastering the grant cycle before and after you win the award, including practical skills in evaluation planning, documentation, and impact reporting.

title: Happiness 2.0 mask workshop – Dec. 11
location: SIDNEY AND LOIS ESKENAZI MUSEUM OF ART
description: Throughout the fall semester, Indiana University undergraduate and high school students from the Bloomington community are invited to participate in the Happiness 2.0 Mask Workshops — an interactive experience that brings together science, art, and reflection on digital life.  The experience combines three components:an accessible discussion of current research on digital media and identity  a guided exploration of artworks in the Eskenazi Museum's galleries  a hands-on mask-making activity    Drawing inspiration from both the research discussion and the museum experience, participants will create a mask representing aspects of their own digital identity and experiences with digital media. Topics explored throughout the workshop include identity formation, online self-presentation, the relationship between online and offline selves, and well-being.

title: Lace Larrabee Returns to Bloomington!
location: The Comedy Attic, 123 S Walnut Street, Bloomington, IN
description: If you haven’t heard of Lace Larrabee, you will soon. Lace is a nationally touring comedian, actress, and host whose debut comedy album, White Trash Cinderella, produced by 800 Pound Gorilla Records, sealed the number one spot on the comedy charts. The accompanying YouTube special amassed over 1.9 million views and counting. A former southern beauty queen, Lace ditched the pageants but kept her dominant stage presence, unrivaled timing and trademark sass. As a season 17 semifinalist on America’s Got Talent, America loved her charming wit so much, NBC brought her back to roast Simon Cowell alongside Roastmaster General himself, Jeff Ross. Lace turned her appearance on AGT into a Vegas residency as host of America’s Got Talent Superstars Live. For over 13 years, Lace has been honing her self-deprecating humor and hilarious personal anecdotes into a style that is fiercely her own. Lace can captivate a room and garner laughs as big as her personality.  From tales of growing up in a trailer to relatable observations on friends, family, love and aging, Lace turns life’s humiliating moments into an indomitable act of comedy. Lace’s candor, perspicacity, and refreshingly real takes on life make comedians want to be her, audiences want to be best friends with her. Lace is a regular favorite on Sirius XM. Lace’s charisma radiates and her writing and delivery are undeniable. Lace has found her voice and is passionate about empowering others to find and use theirs too through founding Atlanta's #1 comedy class, Laugh Lab .

title: Daniel Luis Martinez: The Blueprint | Exhibition
location: The Contemporary Art Museum of Indianapolis
description: Opening reception: Friday, October 2, 2026, 6–10pm  Exhibition on view: October 2–December 18, 2026  For this exhibition, the blueprint is used as both a representational and conceptual departure point. Daniel Luis Martinez uses cyanotype printmaking and mixed-media drawing techniques as a generative process to imagine a speculative home on the CAMi campus. The hybrid drawings and prints featured in the exhibition explore the tactile middle-ground of the blueprint as a creative endeavor.  The series employs orthographic conventions typical of architectural drawing sets, though not as precise instructions for building. Rather, a layered and loose approach expresses ideas of home as an architectonic language.  Daniel Luis Martinez is a registered architect, educator, and co-founder of the multi-disciplinary design studio LAA Office, which explores the intersection of landscape, art, and architecture. His research and creative work investigate the potential of public art to generate alternative forms of placemaking. Martinez is Associate Professor and Director of the IU Eskenazi School's J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program (https://architecture.indiana.edu/index.html) in Columbus, Indiana.  Learn more about the exhibition at the CAMI website (https://camindy.org/exhibitions-all/theblueprint).
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

description: If you haven’t heard of Lace Larrabee, you will soon. Lace can captivate a room and garner laughs as big as her personality.  From tales of growing up in a trailer to relatable observations on friends, family, love and aging, Lace turns life’s humiliating moments into an indomitable act of comedy. Lace’s candor, perspicacity, and refreshingly real takes on life make comedians want to be her, audiences want to be best friends with her. Lace is a regular favorite on Sirius XM. Lace’s charisma radiates and her writing and delivery are undeniable. Lace has found her voice and is passionate about empowering others to find and use theirs too through founding Atlanta's #1 comedy class, Laugh Lab .

title: Rick Springfield
description: Over the past four decades, Rick Springfield has worn many hats as an entertainer and performer. Springfield’s Sirius-XM radio show, Working Class DJ, is a huge hit and airs weekly on 80s on 8. His new album “Automatic” is out now. title: Science of Art: Glass Working
description:
WonderLab is teaming up with the Bloomington Creative Glass Center for Science of Art: Glass Working — and things are about to get hot.

Glass has a secret double life: it cuts, melts, and moves in ways that seem almost magical (spoiler: it's all science). Get hands-on with activities for all ages — try your hand at glass fusing, create a mosaic to take home, or discover the surprising, sweet-toothed properties glass shares with sugar.

Activities:

Glass Fusing

  * Make a Heart, Take a Heart —a fun twist on the usual take-home project. Make an unfinished glass heart to leave behind, then choose a finished one — made by a previous visitor — to take home instead. Your piece then heads to BCGC to be finished, ready for the next person to discover. It's a little chain of glass-making that keeps going, visitor to visitor, round after round.
  * Larger Projects — more involved, creative pieces for older children and adults; pieces are finished off-site by BCGC and available for pickup at their studio. Limited availability.

Mosaics

  * Glass Scoring Station (ages 8+) — try your hand at the scoring techniques used in glasswork
  * Bottlecap & Jar Lid Mosaics — make your own mini mosaic to take home as a pin, magnet, or ornament.

Jolly Rancher Fusion / Suncatcher

  * Use real fused-glass techniques on Jolly Rancher shards to create edible art.
